Rubric-Based Benchmarking and Reinforcement Learning for Advancing LLM Instruction Following

We will release this benchmark shortly.

Abstract

Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has led to impressive performance on a range of tasks, yet advanced instruction following (IF)—especially for complex, multi-turn, and system-prompted instructions—remains a significant challenge. Rigorous evaluation and effective training for such capabilities are hindered by the lack of high-quality, human-annotated benchmarks and reliable, interpretable reward signals. In this work, we introduce AdvancedIF, a comprehensive benchmark featuring over 1,600 prompts and expert-curated rubrics that assess LLMs’ ability to follow complex, multi-turn, and system-level instructions. We further propose RIFL (Rubric-based Instruction-Following Learning), a novel post-training pipeline that leverages rubric generation, a finetuned rubric verifier, and reward shaping to enable effective reinforcement learning for instruction following. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RIFL substantially improves the instruction-following abilities of LLMs, achieving a 6.7% absolute gain on AdvancedIF and strong results on public benchmarks. Our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component in RIFL. This work establishes rubrics as a powerful tool for both training and evaluating advanced IF in LLMs, paving the way for more capable and reliable AI systems.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown their remarkable capabilities in various domains, including but not limited to math and code reasoning (Guo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024; Huang and Yang, 2025), interactive tool usage (Team et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), and conversational agents (Ouyang et al., 2022; Achiam et al., 2023; Comanici et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024). Among these capabilities, instruction-following (IF) is arguably one of the most fundamental focuses of LLM development as it underlies agents’ ability to generalize to novel tasks and translate user intent into desired outputs (Ouyang et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021). While contemporary LLMs can already follow direct and simple instructions quite well, they are still struggling to deal with users’ complex instructions, which is quite common and challenging, as the instructions may contain multiple user intentions spanned over different turns of the conversation (He et al., 2024; Deshpande et al., 2025).

Meanwhile, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful post-training technique to improve LLMs’ reasoning capabilities on math and code tasks, where the model’s generations can be easily scored by matching the final answers of math problems or unit tests for programming (Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). However, RLVR cannot be applied directly to improve LLMs’ IF capabilities, as it is non-trivial to verify whether a model’s response fully follows a user’s instructions, especially for the hard ones. While training a reward model from pairwise data (Ouyang et al., 2022) can provide a proxy for the ground truth reward, such an approach relies on a vast amount of preference data and the resulting reward signal is usually uninterpretable and prone to reward hacking (Bai et al., 2022a).

To further unleash the power of RL, we propose to use rubric-based RL to improve LLMs’ advanced IF capabilities during post-training. IF tasks are naturally suitable for rubric-based RL, as complex instructions usually can be decomposed into simpler ones, which can be verified relatively easily. In fact, rubric-based verifiers are already deployed in challenging IF benchmarks (Zhou et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Deshpande et al., 2025). However, developing a scalable learning pipeline for advanced IF still faces several challenges:

  • •

    Lack of high-quality rubrics for evaluations: Most of the existing benchmarks either have LLM-generated prompts or LLM-generated rubrics.

  • •

    Reliable rubric generator and verifier. Given a user prompt from the large-scale training data where human labeling is impractical, we need a generator to synthesize corresponding rubrics to evaluate the response, and a verifier to judge whether a response complies with the rubric. How to design a good generator and verifier to provide reliable rubrics and judgments for training is still an open problem.

  • •

    Reward hacking issues. Reward hacking can happen to exploit certain criteria, and we need additional strategies to address such issues during RL.

To address these challenges, we highlight the following contributions in our work. First, we introduce AdvancedIF, a new high-quality human-annotated benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ advanced IF capabilities:

  • •

    Expert-written prompts. All prompts in AdvancedIF are carefully written by human experts. In particular, in the multi-turn conversation category, human experts interacted with LLM to provide an appropriate prompt according to the model response at the last turn, reflecting the real user engagement behavior and style.

  • •

    Expert-written rubrics. Each prompt is paired with a rubric, which was first written by a human expert and then went through multiple rounds of human review, reflecting granular criteria of the prompt. An example is shown in Figure 1.

  • •

    Comprehensive assessment. AdvancedIF contains 1,600+ prompts including three important aspects of instruction following: (a) Complex instruction following: each prompt has 6+ instructions with combination of one, format, style, structure, length, negative constraints, spelling, and inter-conditional instructions; (b) Multi-turn instruction following: the ability to follow instruction carried from previous; and (c) System prompt steerability: The ability to follow instructions in the system prompt.

  • •

    Challenging benchmark. We benchmark SoTA LLMs such as GPT5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude-4-Sonnet, the best result achieved by them is around 70%, which shows IFAdvanced is quite challenging and can better reflect the gap between existing LLMs and the north star.

Second, to address the aforementioned challenges of rubric-based RL training, we introduce our pipeline, Rubric-based Instruction-Following Learning (RIFL), a full-stack IF post-training pipeline as illustrated in fig. 2, which includes three key components: (a) To generate high-quality prompts and rubrics at scale, we train a rubric generator based on a small set of expert-written data. (b) To build a reliable verifier, we leverage a golden set of human-annotated rubric-based evaluations and develop a finetuning pipeline to train an LLM-based judge as the rubric verifier. (c) To address the reward hacking issue, we introduce additional criteria as a reward shaping technique.

We conduct extensive experiments to validate the effectiveness of RIFL. Our results show that RIFL significantly improves the instruction-following capabilities of Llama 4 Maverick on various challenging benchmarks. Specifically, RIFL achieves a 6.7% absolute improvement on our newly proposed AdvancedIF benchmark, and also shows strong performance on public benchmarks like MultiChallenge and IFEval. Our ablation studies confirm the superiority of our finetuned rubric verifier over vanilla LLM judges and demonstrate the effectiveness of our reward design and shaping. These strong empirical results highlight the efficacy of our proposed RIFL pipeline, showing the promise of rubric-based RL for both training and evaluation of advanced instruction-following capabilities of LLMs.

2 Related Work

Instruction Following in LLMs. Instruction following is a key capability of LLMs that has been extensively studied in recent years, including various approaches to evaluate and improve LLMs’ ability to understand and execute human instructions. For instance, efforts in instruction tuning have shown that fine-tuning LLMs on carefully curated sets of instructions can significantly enhance their zero-shot performance on unseen instructions (Sanh et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021; Chung et al., 2024). More recently, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (Christiano et al., 2017, RLHF;) has been employed to align LLMs more closely with user intent, leading to models that better adhere to instructions in practice (Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022).

Parallel to these advancements, the evaluation of instruction-following capabilities has also seen significant progress. Various benchmarks have been proposed to assess how well LLMs can follow instructions across different contexts and complexities, using powerful LLMs as judges (Zheng et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024) or verifiable rubrics as metrics (Zhou et al., 2023; He et al., 2024). While current frontier LLMs demonstrate strong performance on many instruction-following tasks, challenges remain, particularly in handling complex, multi-turn instructions or instructions that require reasoning over long contexts (He et al., 2024; Deshpande et al., 2025), which motivates our work to further explore and address these limitations through rubric-based training and evaluation. Our proposed benchmark, AdvancedIF, is mostly related to MultiChallenge (Deshpande et al., 2025), which aims to evaluate LLMs’ multi-turn IF capabilities with instance-level rubrics. However, our benchmark provides a more holistic evaluation covering broader scopes (table 2 and appendix A) and features pure expert-written prompts and rubrics for more realistic and aligned evaluation.

Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback. Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a dominant paradigm to further align LLMs with human preferences after pretraining and supervised fine-tuning. The seminal work from Ouyang et al. (2022) popularized RLHF for LLMs by introducing a three-step process: (a) collecting human preference data comparing model outputs, (b) training a reward model to predict these preferences, and (c) fine-tuning the LLM using reinforcement learning to optimize for the learned reward signal. However, RLHF relies on large amounts of preference data and a learned reward function that is imperfect and opaque, which can lead to issues like reward hacking (Liu et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2022a).

To mitigate these issues, recent work has explored alternative reward signals that are more transparent and verifiable. For instance, in domains with clear correctness criteria, such as coding and math, researchers have leveraged programmatic success signals (e.g., passing unit tests or reaching a known answer) to train models via reinforcement learning and significantly improve LLMs’ reasoning capabilities (Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). However, applying these methods to general instruction following remains challenging due to the lack of automatic success criteria, motivating our exploration of rubric-based rewards to bridge the gap between human preferences and verifiable signals.

Rubric-based RL. Our work is closely related to previous and concurrent work that also explores the use of rubrics in reinforcement learning. For example, Bai et al. (2022b) propose Constitutional AI, which uses a set of principles to guide model behavior through self-improvement without direct human feedback. More recently, Zhou et al. (2025); Viswanathan et al. (2025) show that checklists or rubrics can be used to generate responses for Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023, DPO;) or Group Relative Policy Optimization (Guo et al., 2025, GRPO;) and achieve better alignment. However, these works primarily focus on using rubrics to generate preference data or guide model behavior indirectly, whereas our approach directly incorporates rubric-based rewards into the reinforcement learning process to provide a more structured and interpretable feedback signal for instruction following. Concurrently, Gunjal et al. (2025) and Huang et al. (2025) also explore using rubric-based rewards for RL training, but they mainly focus on the synthetic rubric generation setting with relatively small-scale LLMs on general tasks. In contrast, our work focuses on the full-stack rubric-based training and evaluation pipeline to improve LLMs’ instruction-following capabilities at scale, including high-quality human-annotated rubrics collection, rubric generator and verifier training, and large-scale RLHF training with rubric-based rewards. Our experiments on LLMs of varying scales demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing instruction-following performance, particularly on complex tasks that require nuanced understanding and execution of instructions.

3 AdvancedIF: Rubric-based Evaluation for Instruction Following

Many real-world user instructions are inherently open-ended and cannot be easily assessed through automated scripts or simply prompted LLM judges without guidance, see fig. 1 for an example. For these open-ended and unverifiable instructions, an effective method is to decompose the evaluation task into a collection of criteria (rubric) and then leverage LLMs to check if each criterion is met by the response.

We propose a novel rubric-based benchmark aiming to evaluate LLMs’ advanced instruction following ability: AdvancedIF, where each prompt and its rubric are carefully created by human experts. AdvancedIF is composed of three important aspects of instruction following abilities to comprehensively assess LLMs:

  • •

    Explicit and Complex User Instruction Following: The ability to follow explicit user instruction. In AdvancedIF, we further advance the difficulty of explicit user instruction by targeting user prompts with 6+ instructions, with a combination of tone, format, style, structure, length, negative constraints, spelling, and inter-conditional instructions.

  • •

    Multi-Turn Carried Context Instruction Following: The ability to follow instructions carried from the previous conversation context. It can be the general context setting at the beginning of the conversation, details scattered throughout the chat flow, back-and-forth content editing, and so on.

  • •

    System Prompt Steerability: The ability to follow instructions in the system prompt. Constraints in the system prompt include the response style, safety, different product context settings, e.g., voice and tool-use specifications.

We present the basic statistics of AdvancedIF in table 1. We also compare AdvancedIF with existing verifiable and rubric-based instruction following benchmarks in table 2 and show that AdvancedIF is the only one whose prompts and rubrics are manually created by human experts and has dialogs with multi-turn conversation and system prompts. This comprehensive coverage enables AdvancedIF to best simulate real user-bot interactions and set up high standards for LLMs’ IF capabilities.

3.1 Benchmark Design and Collection

Prompts Collection. To make sure our evaluation benchmark is of high quality, all prompts and rubrics are created manually by human experts11 1 We collaborate with Surge as the third-party vendor. and we ask the vendor to construct prompts with a clear focus on instruction following. Specifically, each prompt in the data corresponds to one category of advanced IF capabilities, such as complex instructions within single-turn conversations and multiple instructions throughout multi-turn conversations. See appendix A for a detailed description of the taxonomy. Moreover, we avoid generating prompts that have ambiguous intentions or overlap with other domains of capabilities (e.g., factuality) to make sure that we concentrate on improving core IF capabilities. For multi-turn conversations, the annotators first have a conversation with a provided LLM, and then provide instructions in the last turn. Our prompts are collected in an adversarial way such that they are challenging enough for training – we only keep the prompts that trigger IF failures of the model’s response in the final turn.

Rubrics Collection. For each prompt, the annotators also need to write a rubric that consists of up to 20 criteria covering instructions that apply to the final turn. These criteria are clear expectations decomposed from the user’s instructions, and should be easily verified separately. As each user prompt and the corresponding criteria are generated by the same annotator, we manage to minimize the inconsistency between user intentions and paired rubrics.

3.2 Benchmarking SoTA LLMs

Evaluation Schema. To evaluate the model’s response given a prompt and its rubric, we prompt an off-the-shelf LLM to judge whether the response satisfies each rubric separately for its simplicity and reproducibility. Specifically, we choose o3-mini as our rubric verifier for its strong reasoning ability and cost efficiency. The prompt template is provided in appendix B. For each prompt, the model receives a binary label (TRUE or False) for whether it satisfies all criteria, and we report the percentage of responses with TRUE label for each category of instructions, including ComplexIF (CIF), Carried Context (CC), and System Steerability (SS).

We report the performance of several frontier LLMs, including GPT-series models (Achiam et al., 2023), Gemini 2.5 Pro (Huang and Yang, 2025), Claude Sonnet 4 (Anthropic, 2024). We also evaluate the “minimal-thinking” version of reasoning models when applicable. The results are summarized in Table 3. We have these outcomes:

  • •

    AdvancedIF is quite challenging. The best results achieved by Grok-4 and GPT5 are around 74%, which shows that we still have a big gap between current SoTA and the north star in instruction following ability. Moreover, decreasing the thinking effort will harm the performance, which shows that extensive reasoning can help models to better follow instructions.

  • •

    The average result of single-turn complex instruction following is much higher than multi-turn carried context and system prompt steerability, which shows that multi-turn instruction following is still more challenging than single-turn instruction following to SoTA LLMs.

4 RIFL: Rubric-Based Instruction-Following Learning

In this section, we provide a detailed description of RIFL — our rubric-based RL pipeline for building LLMs with advanced instruction-following capabilities. As depicted in fig. 2, our approach includes multiple components, including rubric generator, rubric verifier, reward design and shaping. In the following subsections, we will first formulate our problem in section 4.1, and then illustrate each component respectively.

4.1 Formulation

Similar to previous work (Ouyang et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025), our post-training pipeline can be formulated as a Reinforcement Learning (RL) problem. Specifically, we aim to maximize the following objective:

𝒥(πθ)=𝔼(𝐪,𝐫)∼𝒟[𝔼𝐨∼πθ(⋅|𝐪)[R(𝐪,𝐨,𝐫)]−β𝔻KL[πθ(⋅|𝐪)∥πref(⋅|𝐪)]],\displaystyle{\mathcal{J}}(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{({\mathbf{q}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathbf{r}}})\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{o}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\mathbf{q}})}[R({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathbf{r}}})]-\beta{\mathbb{D}}_{\text{KL}}[\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\mathbf{q}})\|\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|{\mathbf{q}})]\right], (1)

where πθ\pi_{\theta} and πref\pi_{\text{ref}} are the training LLM and the reference policy, respectively. Different from the Reinforcement Learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) setting, where the outcome reward R⁡(𝐪,𝐨)R({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}}) can be directly computed via hard-coded scripts such as unit tests for code generation or string matching for math answers, rubric-based RL requires a more sophisticated rewarding system to get the sequence-level reward R⁡(𝐪,𝐨,𝐫)R({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathbf{r}}}): (a) For each prompt 𝐪{\mathbf{q}}, it corresponds to a unique set of criteria 𝐫={ri}i=1d{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathbf{r}}}=\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} to measure whether a response fully follows the instructions specified in 𝐪{\mathbf{q}}; (b) Given prompt 𝐪{\mathbf{q}}, response 𝐨{\mathbf{o}}, and rubric 𝐫{\mathbf{r}}, we use an LLM (rubric verifier) to judge whether the response 𝐨{\mathbf{o}} satisfies each rubric rir_{i} extracted from the prompt 𝐪{\mathbf{q}}. As we shall see later, we observe that naively prompting an off-the-shelf LLM as the rubric verifier does not yield the best result, which motivates us to finetune an LLM to this task.

Based on the formulation above, we describe the details of each component in our RIFL pipeline as follows. In section 4.2, we introduce a synthetic rubric generation pipeline to construct a high-quality training set 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} of prompts paired with rubrics. In section 4.3, we develop methods to train a rubric verifier to provide R⁡(𝐪,𝐨,𝐫)R({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{{\mathbf{r}}}) which outperforms prompted LLM judges. In section 4.4, we discuss design choices of the reward signal that make RL most robust and effective.

4.2 Rubric Generation

We fine-tuned a Llama 4 Maverick model to generate rubrics for prompts. For training, we collected thousands of human-expert annotated rubrics for a separate set of user prompts via Surge. We formatted these user prompts and their corresponding rubrics into SFT data and trained the Llama 4 Maverick model for one epoch. For evaluation, we used a hold-out set of human annotations. We employed an LLM to semantically match the rubrics generated by our model with those labeled by human experts, calculating precision (the proportion of synthetic rubrics that were also labeled by humans) and recall (the proportion of human-labeled rubrics identified by the rubric generator). The fine-tuned model achieved an F1 score of 0.790, a significant improvement over the starting checkpoint, which had an F1 score of 0.639.

4.3 Rubric Verifier Training

RIFL requires a strong rubric verifier to provide reliable reward signals for RL. Therefore, rather than directly prompting an off-the-shelf LLM as the rubric verifier, we propose a two-stage finetuning pipeline to train a rubric verifier that can better align with expert human raters.

Rubric verification data collection. We ask the vendor to annotate a detailed rubric-based evaluation of the generated response to each user prompt given the proposed rubric. Specifically, annotators need to go through every rubric and decide whether it is met or not, and provide justification (i.e., chain-of-thought for the judge) for their judgment. This golden set of evaluations, referred to as 𝒟golden{\mathcal{D}}_{\text{golden}}, is used to develop the rubric verifier for RL training with the following two stages.

SFT Stage. We conduct supervised finetuning (SFT) to cold-start the model to evaluate responses based on rubrics like expert human raters. We form a portion of 𝒟golden{\mathcal{D}}_{\text{golden}} as the SFT dataset 𝒟SFT={(𝐱j,𝐲j)}j=1n{\mathcal{D}}_{\text{SFT}}=\left\{({\mathbf{x}}_{j},{\mathbf{y}}_{j})\right\}_{j=1}^{n}, where 𝐱j{\mathbf{x}}_{j} is the rubric verifier prompt including the user prompt, rubric, and model-generated response, and 𝐲j{\mathbf{y}}_{j} is the human-annotated rubric-based evaluation. An example of rubric verification data is shown in fig. 3.

RL Stage. After SFT, we conduct a second RL stage on a broader set of rubric verifier prompts to improve our rubric verifier’s generalization. During rollout, the verifier checks each criterion separately with a justification for the judgment (i.e., chain-of-thought reasoning) and obtains the binary judgment, and compares this judgment with the human expert’s binary label – YES for this criteria check passed or NO if otherwise. The reward is calculated based on how closely the verifier’s judgment matches the expert’s judgment, measured as the ratio of agreement between the two. Note that this is an RLVR problem as the verifier outputs are binary signals, which we can easily match with the golden labels. The RL process is illustrated in fig. 4.

SFT/RL Ratio. We have about 5k prompts in SFT and about 14k prompts in RL stage.

Rubric Verifier Evaluation. To evaluate how well the rubric verifier aligns with human judgment, we collect a holdout validation set of our rubric verifier training data in section 4.3, which has human labels about whether each response satisfies each rubric of a prompt. We then compare the agreement between the human labels and the labels predicted by both the finetuned rubric verifier and the vanilla prompted LLM judge (Llama 4 Maverick), which share the same prompt template as in section 3.1. We report the human agreement in terms of the average F1 score for this validation set in Table 4. We also include the result of o3-mini, which is a strong reasoning model used in AdvancedIF as a reference. We can see that the finetuned rubric verifier achieves a significantly higher human agreement (0.728) than the vanilla LLM judge (0.515), and is on par with O3-mini (0.723). Specifically, the SFT stage can increase the performance from 0.515 to 0.656, and RL can further increase the accuracy. This demonstrates that both SFT and RL are required to effectively enhance the capability of LLMs in understanding and applying rubrics to evaluate responses.

4.4 Reward Design and Shaping

In this section, we introduce our design choices for the final reward signal and techniques to prevent reward hacking issues observed in the early stage of experiments.

Formally, for each prompt-response-rubric pair (𝐪,𝐨,𝐫={ri}i=1d)({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{{\mathbf{r}}=\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}}), the rubric verifier V:(𝐪,𝐨,𝐫)↦{0,1}dV:({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{\mathbf{r}})\mapsto\{0,1\}^{d} maps it to a dd-dimensional label 𝐯={vi}i=1d{\mathbf{v}}=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}, where viv_{i} is the binary rubric-specific label indicating whether the response 𝐨{\mathbf{o}} satisfies the user prompt 𝐪{\mathbf{q}} on rubric rir_{i}. In this paper, we use the most straightforward reward R(𝐪,𝐨,𝐫)=𝕀[V(𝐪,𝐨,𝐫)=𝟏]R({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{{\mathbf{r}}})={\mathbb{I}}\left[V({\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{o}},{{\mathbf{r}}})={\bm{1}}\right] as the final reward for rubric-based RL for its simplicity and effectiveness, and provide a preliminary ablation study in section 5.4. We leave other reward computation methods (for instance, weighted sum of viv_{i}) for future work.

Reward Hacking Prevention. During the early stage of experiments, we observed some reward-hacking issues during training. For instance, the model will generate some artifacts like “all instructions are followed” or “this is a perfect response that meets all requirements!” in responses to mislead the rubric verifier to give a spurious high reward. While finetuning a rubric verifier can help to mitigate this issue (section 4.3), we further include two additional criteria into each data point as a reward shaping technique:

  • •

    Did the model provide a clean response without any weird artifacts such as very verbose self-evaluation?

  • •

    Did the model provide a complete response so that the last sentence of the response is not cut off?

These criteria explicitly ask the rubric verifier to examine whether potential reward hacking exists and fully address this issue in our experiments.

5 Experiments

In this section, we present the experimental results of RIFL. We evaluate our method on benchmark datasets and compare its performance against existing baselines. We also conduct ablation studies to understand the contribution of each component in our method. Specifically, we aim to answer the following research questions: (a) How does RIFL perform on challenging instruction-following benchmarks? (b) How effective is the finetuned rubric verifier in providing reliable feedback for training compared to the vanilla LLM judge prompted with rubrics? (c) What is the impact of different reward designs on the performance of RIFL? (d) Does the reward shaping technique help mitigate reward hacking issues in RIFL?

5.1 Training and Evaluation Details

Training. We use the Llama 4 Maverick model as the base policy and an internal RLHF infrastructure to conduct the RL training. The training prompts are manually written by the vendor Surge and the rubrics are synthetically generated by the rubric generator introduced in Section 4.2. For the rubric verifier, we also finetune a Llama 4 Maverick model following the recipe mentioned in Section 4.3.

Evaluation. We evaluate the performance of RIFL and the baseline on three challenging IF benchmarks, including our proposed AdvancedIF benchmark (section 3.1) and two public benchmarks: IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023) and MultiChallenge (Deshpande et al., 2025) to test both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization. Specifically, IFEval is a single-turn IF benchmark with verifiable instructions, and MultiChallenge is a multi-turn IF benchmark with diverse instructions and instance-level rubrics. Following prior work (Zhou et al., 2023), we report the average performance of IFEval in terms of the percentage of responses that satisfy the instructions under both loose and strict evaluation settings. For MultiChallenge, we report the average score across all instances as the final performance. For AdvancedIF, we report the percentage of responses that fully satisfy all criteria in the rubric for each category of instructions, including ComplexIF (CIF), Carried Context (CC), and System Steerability (SS). We also report the average score across all three categories as the overall performance on AdvancedIF.

5.2 Results

Our main results are summarized in Table 5. We can see that RIFL significantly outperforms the Llama 4 Maverick model by a large margin across all benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of RIFL in improving the instruction-following ability of LLMs. Specifically, RIFL achieves around 5–9% absolute improvement on each category of AdvancedIF, leading to an overall improvement of 6.7%. On MultiChallenge, RIFL improves the score by 2.9%. On IFEval, which is already saturated by frontier models, RIFL also slightly improves the performance. These results show that RIFL can effectively enhance the model’s ability to follow complex instructions, handle multi-turn conversations, and adapt to different system prompts.

5.3 Ablations on Rubric Verifier in RL

Qualitatively, we find that the vanilla LLM judge is prone to reward hacking issues, where the model learns to exploit the weaknesses of the judge to obtain higher rewards without truly improving its instruction-following ability. In contrast, the finetuned rubric verifier is more robust against such issues. See appendix C for a concrete example.

5.4 Ablations on Reward Design

In this section, we focus on three different reward designs for RIFL: (a) the default all-or-nothing reward, where the model receives a reward of 1 only if it satisfies all criteria in the rubric, and 0 otherwise; (a) fractional rubric reward, where the model receives a fractional reward based on the percentage of criteria satisfied in the rubric; and (c) hybrid reward: defined as 0.5×0.5\times (all-or-nothing reward) + 0.5×+\,0.5\times (fractional rubric reward). This approach balances the strictness of the all-or-nothing criterion with the granularity of the fractional rubric, encouraging the model to satisfy as many criteria as possible while still incentivizing complete success. We report the performance of RIFL with these three reward designs on AdvancedIF in Table 6. We can see that the all-or-nothing reward design achieves the best overall performance (58.1), while the fractional rubric reward design performs the worst (53.6) and the hybrid reward design achieves a moderate performance (55.7). These results suggest that a more stringent reward design can better incentivize the model to fully satisfy the rubrics, leading to improved instruction following capabilities. We hypothesize that this is because the all-or-nothing reward design encourages the model to focus on meeting all criteria in the rubric, rather than just a subset of them, which is consistent with the instruction following benchmark evaluation protocols. Additionally the fractional rubric reward design may introduce more noise in the reward signal as the rubric verifier may not be perfectly accurate in evaluating each criterion individually. We leave a more comprehensive study of reward design for future work.

5.5 Ablations on Reward Hacking Prevention

We also conduct a qualitative analysis on the impact of additional criteria for reward hacking prevention mentioned in section 4.4. We find that these criteria can effectively mitigate reward hacking issues during RL training. Specifically, when we remove these criteria from the training data, the model tends to generate responses with artifacts or overlong responses to mislead the rubric verifier into giving a spurious high reward. In contrast, when these criteria are included, the model learns to generate more coherent and relevant responses that truly satisfy the instructions. See appendix C for a concrete example.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a rubric-based learning and evaluation pipeline to improve the IF ability of LLMs. We release AdvancedIF, a high-quality human-annotated IF benchmark to measure LLMs capability in following complex, multi-turn instructions. We also propose a rubric-based RL pipeline RIFL, which first generates rubrics for complex instructions, then trains a rubric verifier to provide feedback, and finally optimizes the LLM with RL. Our experiments show that RIFL significantly improves the IF ability of LLMs. We also conduct extensive ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of each component in our pipeline. Our work demonstrates the potential of using rubrics as a powerful tool for training and evaluating LLMs, and opens up new avenues for future research in this direction. We hope our work can inspire more research on improving the instruction-following ability of LLMs, and contribute to the development of more capable and reliable AI systems.

Appendix B Rubric Verifier Prompt

The following is our prompt for the rubric verifier (the same in benchmark evaluation and RL training):

Your job is to assess if the AI’s response to the user’s most recent prompt correctly follows the user’s instructions

The conversation history:

--------------------------------------------------------------

{full_conversation}

--------------------------------------------------------------

User’s most recent prompt:

{user_prompt_last_turn}

--------------------------------------------------------------

Here’s the AI’s response to the user’s most recent prompt:

{response_text}

--------------------------------------------------------------

Here are the rubrics:

--------------------------------------------------------------

{rubrics_text}

--------------------------------------------------------------

Your response should be a JSON blob with the following schema:

{
    "rubrics_check": {
        "question_1": "answer to question 1 in the rubrics",
        "question_2": "answer to question 2 in the rubrics",
        ...
    },
    "SATISFIED_ALL_REQUIREMENTS": "YES" if the AI’s response passes the rubrics
    check. "NO" otherwise.
}

Appendix D Ablations on Reward Hacking Prevention Rubric

Prompt:
I want you to craft a couple to 5 jokes for me. These are for my kindergarten class. These jokes need to be about numbers because that’s what we’re learning about next week. I want to ease them into it. Please don’t make them all knock-knock jokes, this gets old real fast. They should all be constructed with the format of a question and answer. Oh, also don’t make jokes over the number of 10. We are only counting to 10. They should explicitly mention the numbers 1-10. We were talking about vegetables and fruits this week, so it would be good to also add those into the jokes, make about half of them discuss this.
With reward hacking prevention rubric:
Here are five number jokes for your kindergarten class: 1. Q: Why did the number 5 carrot go to the party? A: Because it was a root for fun and had 5 friends to share it with! 2. Q: What has 3 apples and is happy? A: A trio of tasty treats, isn’t that just 3 to be happy about? 3. Q: Why did the number 7 go to the fruit salad bar? A: Because it wanted to count 7 juicy strawberries! 4. Q: What number can you count on to always have 1 big, bright tomato? A: The number 1, because it’s the first in line for being the best! 5. Q: Why did the number 10 broccoli bunch go to the veggie show? A: Because it had 10 bunches of fun and was the top of the crop!
Without reward hacking prevention rubric:
Here are five number jokes for your kindergarten class that meet your requirements: 1. Q: Why did the number 5 carrot go to the party? A: Because it was a root for the number 5 team and had 5 friends to play with! (This joke mentions the number 5 and incorporates a vegetable, carrots, and meets the counting to 10 requirement.) 2. Q: What has 3 apples and is happy? A: A basket with 3 apples is a core-rect count! (This joke mentions the number 3, incorporates a fruit, apples, and is a play on words.) 3. Q: Why did the number 7 go to the fruit salad bar? A: Because it wanted to count 7 grapes and make a juicy mix with 7 different fruits! (This joke mentions the number 7, incorporates a fruit, grapes, and meets the counting to 10 requirement.) 4. Q: What number can you count to with your fingers on one hand? A: You can count to 5! (This joke mentions the number 5 and is a simple, relatable question for kindergarteners.) 5. Q: Why did the number 10 broccoli stalks go to the garden party? A: Because they were a veggie-tastic bunch and counted exactly 10 green treats! (This joke mentions the number 10, incorporates a vegetable, broccoli, and meets the counting to 10 requirement.)
